title: The Battle of Bugojno: ARBiH Ascendant in the Vrbas Valley
content:
In mid-July 1993, as fighting between ARBiH and HVO forces intensified across central Bosnia, the ARBiH launched an offensive against HVO-held positions in and around the town of Bugojno, a strategically significant municipality in the upper Vrbas River valley. The battle that followed was one of the most consequential engagements of the Croat-Bosniak war, resulting in ARBiH control of the town and a decisive shift in the military balance across the central Bosnian theater.

Bugojno occupied a critical position in the geography of the conflict. Situated at a junction of the Vrbas valley, the town controlled routes connecting Travnik and Zenica to the north with Gornji Vakuf and Prozor to the south. For the HVO, holding Bugojno was essential to maintaining territorial contiguity between Croat-held areas in Herzegovina and central Bosnia. For the ARBiH, capturing it would consolidate control over the Vrbas valley corridor and sever one of the HVO's key lines of communication.

The ICTY Hadzihasanovic Trial Judgment (IT-01-47-T) addressed the Bugojno operation within its examination of the 3rd Corps command responsibility during the central Bosnian fighting of 1993. The judgment documented the military operations in the area and the subsequent treatment of captured HVO personnel and Croat civilians -- matters that bore directly on the command responsibility charges against General Enver Hadzihasanovic, the 3rd Corps commander.

The attacking force was built around the ARBiH 307th Mountain Brigade, a formation that had been organized and trained in the Bugojno area. The defending HVO unit, the Eugen Kvaternik Brigade, was significantly understrength, able to muster an effective force estimated at only 200 to 400 troops. This disparity reflected the broader problem facing the HVO in central Bosnia: its forces were spread thin across multiple municipalities, facing an ARBiH that was consolidating its numerical superiority through mobilization of the local Bosniak majority population.

Fighting lasted approximately ten days, concentrated in and around the town itself. The ARBiH employed a combination of infantry assault and artillery to reduce HVO positions, and street fighting was intense in several neighborhoods. By the end of July, the HVO garrison had been overwhelmed and the ARBiH had secured control of the municipality. The capture yielded significant quantities of military equipment -- including tanks and artillery pieces -- that were absorbed into the ARBiH inventory, materially improving the 3rd Corps' heavy weapons capability at a time when such equipment was scarce.

The fall of Bugojno had consequences that extended well beyond the town itself. It severed the HVO's ability to maintain coherent defensive lines across central Bosnia, accelerating the fragmentation of Croat-held territory in the region into isolated pockets. HVO forces in Gornji Vakuf, already under pressure, found their northern supply route cut. The broader pattern of the central Bosnian fighting -- in which the ARBiH's greater manpower reserves and interior lines gradually overwhelmed the HVO's smaller but initially better-equipped formations -- was sharply illustrated by the Bugojno outcome.

The aftermath of the battle also produced events that would feature in subsequent ICTY proceedings. The treatment of captured HVO soldiers and detained Croat civilians in the period following the town's capture became a subject of testimony and judicial findings. These proceedings established that abuses occurred against detained persons, matters addressed within the broader framework of command responsibility examined in the Hadzihasanovic trial.

From a strategic perspective, Bugojno demonstrated that the ARBiH had developed the organizational capacity to conduct deliberate offensive operations -- a marked evolution from the improvised defense that had characterized its first year of existence. The 3rd Corps, operating under Hadzihasanovic's command, was becoming an effective conventional military formation capable of concentrating force and seizing objectives. This development carried implications not only for the Croat-Bosniak war but for the broader conflict, as a more capable ARBiH would eventually become a factor in shifting the military balance against the VRS as well.
